biggest_gap.what: RI-PRG04's Clock cost axis is the min on this item and it has never been instrumented. The item's §2 names six consequences of the clock moving — shops open and close (07:00-19:00), the night roster swaps in (21:00-05:00 at +18% damage, +10% aggro, -15% HP and 1.35x souls), NPC schedules move, timed quest windows tick, disease progresses, tide state changes — and the axis's own 10 rung is 'full consequence chain fires' against a 6 rung of 'clock advances and roster swaps'. Across three rounds the aggregation has measured the clock MOVING (rest 12.005093 -> 18.005093, exactly 6 h) and, this round, correctly NOT moving on death (0.000000 h across 150 dead frames, with a delete-the-fix arm returning 0.013889 h). Not one row in any round has measured a consequence. The round's own clock probe tried: reports/runs/W1-13-R3/clock.json names sim/settlement.js#isOpen and sim/npc.js#slotAt in its header, reads getEnvironment().phase (which returns 'night' on both sides of the comparison) and getWorldStats().settlement (which is null because that report has no such key), and ships T5_consumer_moved: false. Under ARBITRATION.md §3 a model with no demonstrated consumer is unmeasurable => 0, and this is the round's headline new model.
biggest_gap.why_it_matters: It is the axis holding RI-PRG04 at 6 and therefore the whole piece below the gate, and it is the Morrowind half of the entire hearth contract — RI-PRG04's own bar says resting 'carries a Morrowind consequence that a bonfire never had: it moves the world's clock, and the world notices'. Today nothing in the measured build shows the world noticing. The consequence is not hypothetical and it is not far away: I drove one of the six myself in four deaths and one kill. With the round's clock fix in place, 4 deaths at 20:58 leave the clock at 20.967593 and an ordinary inf_trash pays 42 souls; with the fix deleted the same 4 deaths walk the clock to 21.023148, across sim/souls.js's NIGHT_FROM_H = 21, and the same kill pays 57 = round(42 x 1.35). That is a world-side consumer changing an entity's behaviour, it took one query, and it also says something the round did not notice: under round 2's clock, DYING REPEATEDLY WAS A WAY TO FARM THE NIGHT RATE, which is the loss-compensation shape RI-JRN06 D9 and AR-1 exist to forbid. The fix is worth more than the round claimed for it and nobody has measured what it is worth.

remedy.action: Add a consequence-chain instrument to tools/journey/jrn06-death.mjs (or to the RI-PRG04 half of it) that rests the world from 17:00 to 23:00 and reads three world-side consumers back, each with the rest removed as its control arm: (a) souls paid for one ordinary kill, off sim/souls.js awardFor(); (b) a merchant's open/closed state, off sim/settlement.js isOpen(); (c) a named NPC's scheduled location, off sim/npc.js slotAt(). Then run the same three arms with game/src/sim/environment.js's `heldByDeath` branch monkeypatched back to the unconditional tick, which turns the same instrument into the CONSUMPTION demonstration reports/runs/W1-13-R3/clock.json is missing. Separately, re-run tools/harness/w1-13-r3-clock.mjs so its stored verdict matches the predicate now in the tree — T5_consumer_moved reads false in the file and evaluates true on the file's own numbers.
remedy.acceptance: A new aggregation row reports, in one run: souls_per_ordinary_kill 1.35x higher after the rest than before it and 1.00x in the no-rest control; at least 1 merchant with is_open true before the rest and false after; at least 1 named NPC whose slotAt() location differs across the rest; and, in the death arm, 4 deaths at 20:58 moving the clock 0.000000 h with the fix in and >= 0.05 h with it out, with the same-kill souls award differing between those two arms. RI-PRG04's Clock cost axis then has evidence for every clause of its own 6 rung and at least three of the six consequences its 10 rung names.

secondary_observations.what: THE ROUND-3 RENDERER CHANGE IS INERT, and the arm that shows it was written by the builder and left switched off. Round 3 answered the named gap two ways: it changed the M-D14 camera, and it committed game/src/render/renderer.js (0b2d6ef) lifting the bloom onto the DRAWN ground via _drawnGroundY and giving it a 1.9 m cross-planed hum, justified in a long comment on the grounds that 'a 0.37 m object seen from an eye 1.6 m up at 12 m is a 1.8-degree target behind several metres of 0.34 m relief'. The probe's own pre-r3-render arm removes both — _drawnGroundY re-pointed at its own fallback, the hum blades detached from the group — and shoots the corrected camera at the pre-round-3 bloom. It reads 8/8 daylight at 12 m and 8/8 dark at 6 m, identical to the shipped renderer: ZERO bearings bought, in either condition. With a camera at a standing person's eye the knot, cap and halo alone read from every bearing. RULES.md 6 is 'delete-the-fix … then check the two arms actually differ — an inert fix has passed here twice'; this would be the third, and the builder wrote the arm that catches it and did not run it. The remedy is not to delete the hum — it is depthTest:true geometry that real terrain occludes, m_d19 confirms it is not a marker, and a column of sap-light on a bloodstain is defensible art direction — it is to stop documenting art direction as a fix, or to find the condition where it earns its place.

The 2x2 the round left unrun says the M-D14 camera's EYE was the whole story and its AIM was nothing — so the builder guessed the right factor and described the wrong mechanism, and was right to refuse to claim either. At bearing 0, 12 m, hour 12, one bloom, one browser, four poses each against its own 180-degree-away control: OLD eye + OLD aim margin 0 (BLIND); OLD eye + NEW aim margin 0 (BLIND); NEW eye + OLD aim margin 4,324 (READS); NEW eye + NEW aim margin 4,264 (READS). The 0.8 m of aim buys nothing and the 0.19 m of eye buys everything — marginally more on its own than the round-3 camera does. The build's first explanation, that the old eye was buried under the drawn ground, was correctly refuted by its own eye_above_observer_ground_m of 1.346-1.705 m; the actual mechanism is visible in the shot, where the top two panels are flat grey because the eye is INSIDE A BOULDER and 19 cm clears it.

engine.projectPoint() is blind to every posed camera in the project, and it fails plausibly rather than loudly. engine.camera({pos, look}) (engine.js:5669-5683) writes c.override, c.pos, c.pivot and c.fov and NEVER writes c.yaw or c.pitch; projectPoint (engine.js:5750) calls projectNDC -> sim/camera.js project() -> viewBasis(c), which builds the basis from c.yaw/c.pitch alone. Measured at four bearings with the camera posed at an observer's eye and aimed at the drawn bloodstain: pos_was_applied true on 4 of 4, and the yaw the projection used was 15 degrees on all four against poses implying -90, 180, 90 and 0. Pixels say the bloom is on screen at 4 of 4 (1,075-4,777 amber px); projectPoint says on_screen at 1 of 4 — the bearing where the stale yaw happened to be nearly right — and at bearing 180 it returns in_front: true with an NDC x of 4.42. The build tripped over this: all 96 rows of its own bloom-sight.json carry projected.on_screen false, including sixteen rows scored visible at up to 27,134 px of margin, and the file's header sells that read as 'a shape that cannot lie the way a single count can'. This is not W1-13's model, but it lands on NEXT-DISPATCH.md §1a's standing instruction to re-read visual verdicts taken through a posed camera: any of them that asked projectPoint whether something was in frame was told no.

path_to_ten item 8 measured live rather than read: with the inventory screen open at settlement_primary_street, the DRAWN inventory.gold element reads '0 gold' before setGold(777) and '0 gold' after. engine.js:3345 is still `gold: (this.sim.loadout && this.sim.loadout.gold) || this.sim.gold || 0` and neither field is ever defined on the sim, exactly as round 2 reported. The build declares the item untouched and assigns it to W1-15/W1-21, which is honest and is also not a closure: no arbitration question for it exists in orchestration/, so the line has no owner who can close it.

m_d2b_placement_rules_exercised under-counts its own aggregation, in the safe direction. Its rules_over_the_whole_journey key is built at jrn06-death.mjs:782 from the scripted twenty plus its own two world-driven rows, and m_d3_unreachable_relocation — which reports placement_rule 'relocated_toward_hearth', relocated_m 14.5 — runs later in the same file. So the shipped run exercises 4 of the 5 declared placement rules and the build reports 3. The remaining unreached rule is clamped_within_2m (death.js:278).

The in-row 180-degree-away control in M-D14 is a constant, not a scene-varying control. control_px is 195 in every one of the 96 probe rows and every one of the 24 aggregation rows, at both hours, on every bearing, with and without a bloom in the world: it is the HUD's own amber (renderer.uiVisible defaults true and hud.health/stamina/focus/heal/equipload/quickslots draw in every shot), and the marsh contributes exactly zero pixels in the detector's band from any direction. It still functions — a detector firing on scenery would raise it — but the control doing real work in this round is the one the build added: drink the bloom and re-shoot, which returns 8 x 195 px at max margin 0. That one covers the dark condition only; daylight, whose margins are 40x smaller, has no world-driven null control.

The leg that leaves the inventory screen open is still not fixed; it is gated. world_runs_legs_jrn06-death reports ui_mode_on_entry 'inventory' in the shipped run, between frame 70 (where the previous gate site saw 'world') and frame 201. Round 2 asked for both the central gate AND the leg; the gate landed and is genuinely journey-agnostic (world-runs-gate.mjs, imported at three sites in journey-run.mjs plus jrn06-death.mjs), so no journey can now measure a frozen world — but the leg is still opening a screen and walking away from it, and the next instrument to grow in that window inherits the defect.

Three of the round's five artifacts carry no git field at all (levelling.json, levelling-r3b.json, drift.json) and two more carry a git_stamp_note explaining that they predate the stamp (bloom-sight.json, clock.json). RULES.md 12 is 'stamp the commit on every number'. The build fixed the tools mid-round so later runs self-stamp — my re-run of its own bloom-sight.mjs carries a git block — and it declined to back-date a commit it had not captured, which is the right call. But three of the files backing path_to_ten items 3, 4 and 5 are unstamped.

journey-run.mjs's top-level ok is !led.anyUnmeasurable — a COVERAGE statement, not a failure one — and two consecutive rounds of this piece have read it as two different things. Round 2 wrote 'I ran the aggregation the builder could not, and it says ok: false' as a failure headline (it coincided with two red instruments); round 3 correctly says the same false is not a failure (zero red instruments, four unmeasurable, three of which the build itself declares absent in getCapabilityReport().harness_amendments_absent). The build's reading is fair on the field as written and I checked the line rather than the claim. A field that two honest readers read oppositely should be split into ok_pass and ok_coverage.

A neighbour's `git add -A` staged this verdict and its artifacts while I was writing them — RULES.md 17's exact failure mode. Nothing of W1-13's was staged for deletion and no measurement is affected. Recorded because the rule exists because it has bitten before.

arbitration_questions.question: Does RI-JRN06 M-D8's 'exactly one bloodstain, always' hold when the second death happens ON the basin the player respawns at, so the freshly placed 0-soul bloom is drunk at range 0 inside the respawn window?
arbitration_questions.souls_side: The letter says a stain exists after every death. Dark Souls places a 0-soul stain and the player can see it.
arbitration_questions.morrowind_side: Nothing is lost and nothing is duplicated: the bloom WAS placed and the player WAS standing on it, so recovering it instantly is the loop working, not the loop failing. (1) The bloom arms: I re-ran the build's own probe on the current tree and reproduced as-placed 2/8 + 3/8 and player-eye 8/8 + 8/8 to the bearing, then ran the three arms it left switched off. (2) The aggregation's tally: 42 instruments, 23 pass, 0 fail, 4 unmeasurable, counted off the file. (3) The pool fix's consumer: measured at the entity level with a 700-damage blow, survived at 828 and lethal at 620. (4) The clock fix's consumer: measured through sim/souls.js's 21:00 night window, 42 souls shipped against 57 with the fix deleted.
self_audit.how: Every arm in critic-w1-13-r3.mjs carries its delete-the-fix counterpart in the same browser on identical frames, and both are reported: C1's fix-deleted arm dies where the shipped arm lives, C4's fix-deleted arm crosses the night window where the shipped arm does not. C2 is itself a falsification of an instrument the round relied on — I checked the pose WAS applied (pos_was_applied true on 4 of 4) before concluding the projection was the broken half, so 'the camera never moved' is ruled out. And I checked the no-bloom null control could not be silently undone by a re-render before trusting it.

self_audit.self_audit_note: ran_every_assigned_method is FALSE and the reasons are in method_deviations: I did not re-run the aggregation, and I did not recompute spacing, S7, m_d3, m_d15 or m_d16. Every one of those is either carried at round 2's score and marked as carried, or scored fail-closed. Escalation ladder, all five rungs, on a round whose headline was 'the previous critic was wrong': (1) ZOOM — took the two arms of the 2x2 the build left unrun and the delete-the-fix arm for the renderer, rather than accepting a three-arm result; (2) CHANGE THE SAMPLE — measured the pool fix by what a BODY does under a blow rather than by what a field says, and the clock fix by what an ENEMY pays rather than by what the clock reads; (3) STRESS — chose a blow (700) that sits strictly between the unlevelled ceiling and the levelled one, so the arms cannot agree by luck, and a fixture (20:58, four deaths) that crosses a threshold in exactly one arm; (4) SECOND-ORDER PROPERTY — not 'did the number move' but 'is there a world-side reader', which is where clock.json's own T5 says false and my arm says 42 -> 57; (5) FIRST MINUTE AND TENTH HOUR — in the first minute a player now dies, walks back and sees the light on the floor from any direction they approach from, which is new and real; in the tenth hour the clock they have been resting into has still never been shown to close a shop, move an NPC or swap a roster, which is what the whole Morrowind half of the hearth was for.
